name: Taíno
info: The Taíno were the Indigenous farming peoples of the Greater Antilles, the Bahamas and the northern Lesser Antilles, ruled by caciques; the first people Columbus met in 1492, they live on in their descendants today.

facts.homeland: The Lucayan Archipelago (the Bahamas), Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola (Haiti and the Dominican Republic) and Puerto Rico, east to Guadeloupe; ceremonial grounds such as Tibes in Puerto Rico.
facts.period: Ceramic Age ancestors entered the Caribbean c. 2,500 years ago; Taíno chiefdoms met the Spanish in 1492; Spanish documents called them extinct by 1550, but their descendants and revival communities live on today.
facts.known: chiefdoms (cacicazgos) ruled by caciques; matrilineal succession; worship of zemís; cassava grown in conuco mounds; the batey ball game; dugout canoes and cotton hammocks; words such as hammock, canoe, tobacco and hurricane
facts.sources: Spanish chroniclers (Christopher Columbus, Ramón Pané, Bartolomé de las Casas, Peter Martyr d’Anghiera); excavated villages, ball courts, zemís and petroglyphs; DNA studies of ancient and living people; oral histories of descendant communities.

t: The Taíno lived in villages of large round houses around a central plaza, farmed cassava in heaped mounds and were ruled by caciques, whose office usually passed through the female line.
Their religion centred on zemís, spirits and ancestors given form in carved wood, stone, shell and cotton, and honoured with cohoba snuff, songs and ceremonies.
Spanish conquest after 1492 brought forced labour, war and epidemics that killed most Taíno within decades, yet Taíno descent, customs and identity survive in the Caribbean today.
dyk: The English words barbecue, hammock, canoe, tobacco, savanna and hurricane all come from Taíno words: barbacoa, hamaca, kanoa, tabaco, sabana and juracán.
ev: Pottery-making farmers of the Ceramic Age, ancestors of the Taíno, enter the Caribbean from north-eastern South America
A woman later studied as an “ancient Taíno” lives in the Bahamas; her genome was mapped in 2018
Christopher Columbus lands in the Bahamas, on the island the Taíno called Guanahaní
On his second voyage Columbus begins to demand tribute in gold and cotton from the Taíno of Hispaniola
Caciques of Puerto Rico, among them Agüeybaná II, rise against the Spanish, while Antonio de Montesinos denounces the enslavement of the islanders
The cacique Hatuey, who had fled from Hispaniola to Cuba to unite its peoples, is burned at the stake
Enriquillo leads more than 3,000 Taíno in a successful rebellion on Hispaniola and wins land and a royal charter
9,399 people in Puerto Rico identify as Taíno in the United States census

sections.origins:
The people now called the Taíno lived across most of the West Indies when Europeans arrived, from the Lucayan Archipelago through Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico to Guadeloupe. They spoke an Arawakan language and are also called Island Arawaks or Antillean Arawaks. Taíno was not the name they gave themselves: Columbus simply called the islanders “Indians”, and Constantine Samuel Rafinesque first used the word for them in 1836. It comes from nitaino, the name of an elite class, which José Barreiro translates as “men of the good”. Scholars such as Basil Reid, José Oliver and L. Antonio Curet warn that the label covers many groups with different languages and identities; Irving Rouse divides the historic Taíno into Classic, Western and Eastern Taíno.

The Taíno creation story says that the first people came out of caves in a sacred mountain on Hispaniola. Scholars have offered two theories of where their ancestors came from. One traces them to Arawak speakers of the central Amazon Basin who moved down the Orinoco Valley and along the Lesser Antilles; the other, the circum-Caribbean theory of Julian H. Steward, derives them from the Colombian Andes. DNA studies suggest that the Taíno descended from a wave of pottery-making farmers, the Ceramic Age people, who entered the Caribbean from north-eastern South America about 2,500 years ago and met the earlier Archaic Age people, who had arrived some 6,000 or 7,000 years ago.

The two groups seem not to have intermarried often, though Archaic Age people may have survived in western Cuba until around 900 CE, and pottery and DNA from Puerto Rico and Hispaniola point to both Ceramic and Archaic origins. What is known of the Taíno comes from Spanish chroniclers such as Bartolomé de las Casas and the friar Ramón Pané, from excavated villages, ball courts and carvings, and from DNA studies of ancient and living people.
sections.society:
The Taíno lived in villages, called yucayeques, under a chief known as a cacique, or cacica when the ruler was a woman, and grouped their chiefdoms, the cacicazgos, into confederations. Spanish chroniclers described four classes: the cacique, the nitaínos, the bohíques and the naborias. The nitaínos were nobles, warriors and the cacique’s family, from whom the cacique’s advisers were chosen; the naborias were the more numerous working people. Chiefs were chosen from the nitaínos and generally owed their power to a maternal line: Las Casas and Peter Martyr d’Anghiera reported that a chief was succeeded by a son of his sister. A cacique’s power rested on the villages he controlled and on alliances of family, marriage and ceremony, and Pané wrote that the principal caciques had as many as 10, 15 or 20 wives.

Women lived in village groups with their children and held extensive control over their lives; they could rule as cacicas, served as food producers and ritual specialists when men were at war, and the wealthiest gathered crafted goods for trade and gifts. Most people lived in large round houses, bohíos, of wooden poles, straw and palm leaves, each holding 10–15 families, built around a central plaza used for games, festivals and ceremonies; the cacique’s family lived in a rectangular house, the caney. Settlements in Puerto Rico and Hispaniola were the largest, those in the Bahamas the smallest.

Farming fed this society. Cassava (yuca) was planted with a wooden digging tool, the coa, in heaped mounds called conucos, which drained the soil and let roots be stored in the ground; women squeezed the poison out of cassava and ground it into flour for bread. Sweet potato, maize, squash, beans, peppers, peanuts and pineapples were grown too, and the Taíno fished with nets, weirs and spears, hunted hutias, birds and iguanas, and kept fish and turtles alive in weirs until they were eaten.
sections.beliefs:
Taíno spirituality centred on zemís, spirits or ancestors. Among the greatest were Atabey, the zemí of the moon, fresh waters and fertility, and her son Yúcahu, the spirit of cassava and the sea, whom the Taíno of Hispaniola called “White Yuca, great and powerful as the sea and the mountains”. Guabancex, the destructive aspect of Atabey, ruled storms and hurricanes; Boinayel and Márohu brought rain and fair weather; Maquetaurie Guayaba ruled Coaybay, the land of the dead, which the dog-shaped zemí Opiyelguabirán watched over. The Taíno believed they descended from the cultural hero Deminán Caracaracol and a female turtle.

Zemí was also the name for the objects that gave these beings form, made mostly of wood but also of stone, bone, shell, pottery and cotton, and carved as petroglyphs on rocks, in ball courts and on cave stalagmites. Three-pointed stones representing Yúcahu were placed in the conucos to increase the cassava harvest. Some zemís stood with small trays believed to have held cohoba, a hallucinogenic snuff made from the beans of a tree, which was inhaled through carved tubes. The priests, the bohíques, fasted and took sacred tobacco snuff before speaking with the gods, healing the sick and interpreting the will of the spirits for the community.

Before some ceremonies people purified themselves by fasting or by inducing vomiting with a swallowing stick; communal bread was then served first to the zemí, then to the cacique and then to everyone, and the village sang its epic to maracas and other instruments. In the areítos held in the plaza the deeds of the ancestors were celebrated. Taíno stories told that the Sun and Moon came out of caves, that the oceans poured from a gourd holding the bones of Yayael, the son of the great spirit Yaya, and that the souls of the dead rested in Coaybay by day and went out at night as bats to eat guavas.
sections.arts:
Taíno craftspeople carved zemís in wood, stone, bone and shell, and drew their faces, toads, turtles, fish and snakes on pottery and in tattoos. Caciques sat on carved wooden seats, duhos, raised above their guests, and wore tunics of cotton and rare feathers, crowns, cotton masks with feathers, shells or gold, woven belts and necklaces of snail beads. Their mark of office was the guanín, an ornament of gold and copper alloy of South American origin, which stood for the first mythical cacique, Anacacuya, “star of the centre”. Homes held cotton hammocks, palm mats, wooden chairs and cradles.

Men made fishing nets and ropes of cotton and palm and hollowed dugout canoes, kanoa, that held from 2 to 150 people, an average one 15–20. They hunted with bows and arrows tipped with poison and made wooden war clubs called macanas. Fishers tied a remora to a line, let it fasten onto a larger fish or a turtle and dived to retrieve the catch, or stunned fish with crushed senna plants. Farmers grew tobacco, cotton and calabashes around their houses and smoked tobacco in pipes and cigars or inhaled it as powder through a tube. Maize was eaten off the cob and brewed into a drink, chicha.

The Taíno played a ceremonial ball game, batey, with teams of 10 to 30 players and a solid rubber ball, in village plazas or on rectangular courts; the most elaborate courts lie on the boundaries between chiefdoms, and games are believed to have settled disputes between communities. Petroglyphs at Taíno sites have been described as an early form of proto-writing. Their words entered other languages: barbacoa (barbecue), hamaca (hammock), kanoa (canoe), tabaco (tobacco), sabana (savanna) and juracán (hurricane).
sections.exchange:
When Europeans arrived the Taíno shared their islands with older peoples, the Guanahatabeys of western Cuba and the Ciguayos and Macorix of Hispaniola, and were in conflict with the Caribs of the southern Lesser Antilles, who raided Puerto Rico and captured women; Taíno communities allied to defend themselves. On 12 October 1492 Christopher Columbus landed in the Bahamas, on an island the Taíno called Guanahaní, and described the islanders as gentle and generous. In 1494 about 24 Taíno were abducted and taken to Spain. From 1493 Columbus demanded tribute in gold or spun cotton from every adult on Hispaniola, and those who failed to pay were brutally punished, which provoked many revolts.

Under the encomienda system the Spanish forced the Taíno to work in fields and mines and seized their land. In 1511 the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos became the first European to denounce this enslavement publicly. That year caciques of Puerto Rico, among them Agüeybaná II and Urayoán, allied with the Caribs against the Spanish, but the revolt was put down by Juan Ponce de León. Hatuey, who had fled from Hispaniola to Cuba with 400 people, was burned at the stake on 2 February 1512, while on Hispaniola Enriquillo led more than 3,000 Taíno in a successful rebellion in the 1520s and won land and a charter from the crown.

Within 30 years between 80 and 90 per cent of the Taíno died. How many there had been is uncertain: estimates for Hispaniola range from 10,000 to 1,000,000, and a 2020 genetic study suggested no more than a few tens of thousands. Many historians blame epidemics of smallpox, influenza, measles and typhus above all; others, such as Andrés Reséndez, argue that enslavement and forced labour in the mines were a major killer, and David Stannard calls the encomienda a genocidal system. A famine in 1495–1496, when some Taíno refused to plant to frustrate the Spanish, killed some 50,000.
sections.legacy:
Spanish documents declared the Taíno extinct as early as 1550, and histories of the Caribbean long repeated it. Yet many survived through marriage and flight: census records of 1514 show that 40 per cent of Spanish men on Hispaniola had Taíno wives, and on Jamaica Taíno men and women fled to the Blue Mountains, where they joined escaped enslaved Africans among the ancestors of the Jamaican Maroons. Puerto Rico’s censuses of 1777 and 1787 still listed 1,756 and 2,032 indios. In eastern Cuba, around El Caney, Yateras and Baracoa, observers from the 19th century onwards recorded Indigenous communities, and some have kept a Taíno identity into the 21st century.

DNA studies show that 61 per cent of Puerto Ricans, up to 30 per cent of Dominicans and 33 per cent of Cubans carry mitochondrial DNA of Indigenous origin, inherited through the female line, and rural Dominicans keep Taíno farming, food, fishing, medicine and building traditions. Since the late 20th century descendants have reclaimed the name Taíno, or Boricua in Puerto Rico, describing traditions passed down in secret; by 2006 a couple of dozen organisations from Florida to Puerto Rico and California to New York formed what is called the Taíno restoration. In the 2010 United States census 9,399 people in Puerto Rico identified as Taíno. The Yamaye Guani Taíno People speak for Jamaica’s Taíno, the governor of the US Virgin Islands has recognised the Guainía Taíno Tribe, and some groups are rebuilding a Taíno language, Taíney.

Scholars still disagree about how much Taíno culture survived. Some point to the mixing of peoples over centuries as evidence against survival; descendants answer that mixing is how their culture lasted, and Curet agrees that it “does not disprove the claims of indigenous survival”, while warning that it can downplay African heritage. Taíno history is now taught in Puerto Rico’s schools.

summary: The Taíno were the Arawakan-speaking peoples of the Greater Antilles, the Bahamas and the northern Lesser Antilles, who farmed cassava, lived in villages ruled by caciques and honoured zemís. They were the first people of the Americas met by Columbus in 1492. Spanish forced labour, war and disease killed most of them within decades, but their descendants and revival communities keep a Taíno identity alive today.

end: kept null. The article opens by saying Taíno culture “has been continued today by their descendants and by Taíno revivalist communities” and gives a long section on present-day Taíno; the legacy section presents both the descendants’ view and the scholars’ scepticism, as the article does.

start: kept 1200 (circa). The article gives no date for the start of Taíno culture as such: the Ceramic Age ancestors came c. 2,500 years ago, the islands “supported a high number of people for approximately 1,500 years”, and an “ancient Taíno” genome is 8th–10th century. 1200 is not contradicted, but nothing in the article supports it specifically; the editor may prefer an earlier date (e.g. c. 600 CE).

Left out: the details of the punishment for unpaid tribute (cut-off hands, from Kirkpatrick Sale) are summarised as “brutally punished”; Las Casas’s figure of three million dead, which researchers today call an exaggeration; Jason Hickel’s estimate of deaths in the mines.
The article says Taíno women lived in village groups with their children and “men lived separately”; this sits oddly beside its account of avunculocal residence. I kept only the first claim, briefly.
The article names Bartolomé de las Casas as having lived in Santo Domingo and arrived in 1508; not used.
